slides.title: Why AI for MBA Students
slides.text:
Why AI for MBA Students
1. Awareness & Curriculum Integration
Over 75% of business schools worldwide (including India and the U.S.) now weave AI into their curricula—from tutoring to strategy and career guidance
(Leading schools like Wharton, Kogod, Columbia, Duke, Stanford, and Harvard actively embed AI tools into core subjects. 2. AI Skills Demand
74% of employers specifically look for AI/ML proficiency in MBA grads, lifting AI from 21st to 4th among sought-after competencies (e-GMAT).
66% of organizational leaders won’t hire candidates lacking AI literacy (Microsoft CDN).
Recruiters note AI fluency is now expected more than ever, especially for roles involving strategy and operations (AI Literacy Institute).

3. Practical Usage & Engagement
Students use AI weekly, if not daily, for essay writing, brainstorming, data analysis, simulations and more .
Schools report AI-enabled projects, workshops, and hackathons (e.g., datathons with Bloomberg, Amazon) to boost hands-on experience (Study International). 4. Gaps & Challenges
While AI adoption is high, formal training remains inconsistent; e.g., UK study shows only 36% of students receive institutional support in 2025 .
MBA programs face challenges like lack of strategy, ethics integration, and equipment for deep AI use (globalfocusmagazine.com).

slides.title: What is Artificial Intelligence
slides.text:
What is Artificial Intelligence
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science focused on creating systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence. These tasks include learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and decision-making

bullets.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science focused on creating systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence. These tasks include learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and decision-making

slides.title: Definition of AI:
slides.text:
Definition of AI:
Artificial Intelligence is the science and engineering of making intelligent machines, especially intelligent computer programs. It aims to create systems that can mimic human intelligence by performing tasks such as reasoning, learning, problem-solving, understanding language, and perception.
Example Source: John McCarthy (who coined the term AI in 1956) defined it as: “The science and engineering of making intelligent machines.”

bullets.text: Artificial Intelligence is the science and engineering of making intelligent machines, especially intelligent computer programs. slides.title: Modern Definition of AI
slides.text:
Modern Definition of AI
Artificial Intelligence refers to the development of computer systems or machines that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence. These tasks include understanding natural language, recognizing patterns, making decisions, generating content, adapting through learning (machine learning), and even interacting with humans in real time.
In today’s context, AI includes powerful subfields like machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and generative AI.
Example Modern View (by experts like Russell and Norvig):
“AI is the study of agents that perceive their environment and take actions that maximize their chances of achieving their goals.”

slides.title: Core Capabilities of AI
slides.text:
Core Capabilities of AI
Learning: Adapting behavior based on data and experience (e.g., machine learning, deep learning).
Reasoning: Drawing conclusions from available information.
Perception: Interpreting sensory input like images, sounds, or text.
Language Understanding: Communicating in human languages (natural language processing).
Decision-Making: Choosing actions based on goals and context.

slides.visual_text: Infographic titled The Evolution of AI: A Journey Through Time, subtitle: From the question "Can machines think?" to AI that creates, understands, and empowers. Five columns joined by arrows. 1. Thinking About Intelligence (1950): Can machines imitate human thinking? Alan Turing proposed the Turing Test to measure machine intelligence; a black-and-white portrait beside a small Turing Test icon (person, question mark, computer). Key contribution: laid the theoretical foundation of Artificial Intelligence. 2. Rule-Based Conversation (1960s to 1970s): chatbots like ELIZA and PARRY followed predefined rules; an old computer screen reading ELIZA, How do you feel today? and a robot icon labelled PARRY; these systems could simulate conversation but had no real understanding or learning. Key contribution: first conversational AI programs; demonstrated the human tendency to attribute intelligence to machines. 3. Knowledge and Learning (1980s to 2000s): expert systems and machine learning enabled AI to learn from data; AI moved from hard-coded rules to learning patterns and making predictions. Key contribution: learning from data; expert systems for decision support; early machine learning algorithms. 4. Deep Learning (2012 onwards): neural networks achieved breakthroughs in vision, speech and language (a neural network drawing with Vision, Speech and Language icons); deep learning scaled with big data and powerful computing. Key contribution: breakthrough performance in complex tasks; enabled real-world applications (e.g., image recognition, voice assistants). 5. Generative AI (2022 onwards): Large Language Models such as ChatGPT can understand context, generate content, analyze data, write code, and support business decision-making (icons for Content Generation, Data Analysis, Code Generation, Business Decision Support around a round knot-shaped logo); AI is now accessible to millions of users across industries. Key contribution: human-like understanding; multi-task capabilities; democratization of AI. Bottom banner: The journey of AI is a journey of expanding capability: Can machines think? to Can machines talk? to Can machines learn? to Can machines understand? to Can machines create and empower?

slides.visual_text: The three bullets in the slide text, plus a picture timeline of conversational machines: Alan Turing Machine (1950, a typewriter-like machine), ELIZA (1965, an old computer), PARRY (1972, a medal), Cathrine (1991, a cartoon face of a woman), Eugene Goostman (2000, a cartoon face of a boy) and Cleverbot (2011, a smiling cloud).

Infographic titled The Journey of Artificial Intelligence. A timeline across the top: 1950 Birth of AI; 1956 Dartmouth Conference; 1960s to 1970s AI Winters; 1980s Expert Systems Rise; 1990s to 2000s Machine Learning Emerges; 2010s Deep Learning Breakthrough; 2020s and Beyond Foundation Models and Generative AI. Main panel, beside a portrait signed Alan Turing: 1. 1950, Alan Turing and the Birth of AI. The journey of AI began in 1950 when Alan Turing published his landmark paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." Instead of asking "Can machines think?" he proposed a practical test called the Turing Test. Three boxes. Turing Test (drawing of a human, a human evaluator at a screen, and a machine): a human communicates with both another human and a machine through text; if the evaluator cannot reliably distinguish the machine from the human, the machine is considered to exhibit intelligent behavior. Significance: introduced the concept of machine intelligence; laid the theoretical foundation for Artificial Intelligence; inspired decades of AI research. Limitation (a mask beside a speech bubble with a red cross): the machine only needs to imitate human conversation; it does not necessarily understand what it is saying. Bottom line: Alan Turing's idea in 1950 was the spark that ignited the journey of AI, transforming science fiction into scientific pursuit.

Infographic titled 2. 1966, ELIZA: The First Chatbot, with a portrait signed Joseph Weizenbaum. ELIZA was created at MIT by Joseph Weizenbaum. ELIZA simulated a psychotherapist by asking reflective questions. It worked using simple pattern matching rather than genuine understanding. Example box: User: I feel stressed. ELIZA: Why do you feel stressed? Despite its simplicity, many users felt that ELIZA "understood" them! Contribution: first successful chatbot; demonstrated that humans easily attribute intelligence to computers; introduced conversational interfaces. How ELIZA worked: a terminal screen (Welcome to ELIZA. Type your messages and press Enter. YOU: I feel stressed. ELIZA: Why do you feel stressed? YOU: I have a lot of work to do. ELIZA: Can you explain more about your work? YOU: I have too many deadlines. ELIZA: Why do you have too many deadlines?). ELIZA looked for keywords and used predefined rules to generate responses. It did not understand meaning. Limitation (a crossed-out sad robot): ELIZA had no memory, no reasoning, no learning; it simply matched keywords. Bottom line: ELIZA was a milestone that showed conversation was possible, even without real understanding.

Infographic titled 3. 1972, PARRY: Simulating Human Behavior. Developer: Kenneth Colby (portrait signed Kenneth Colby). PARRY was developed to simulate a patient with paranoid schizophrenia. Unlike ELIZA, PARRY included internal beliefs and emotional states. Instead of simply matching words, it modeled suspicion, fear and emotions (drama masks icon). This made conversations appear much more realistic. Example conversation: User: Why do you think people are watching you? PARRY: I'm not sure... sometimes I feel they are against me... they talk about me... I can't trust them. User: Who are they? PARRY: People in the hospital... even my doctor... maybe everyone. What happens inside PARRY? (a head containing Beliefs, Emotions, Goals, Suspicion): has beliefs about others; feels emotions; shows suspicion and fear; responds based on its internal state. PARRY went beyond surface patterns: it simulated a mind with feelings and beliefs. Contribution: added psychological modeling; introduced primitive reasoning; more believable than ELIZA.

Infographic titled 4. 1991, CATHERINE: A Step Forward in Conversational AI. An old computer screen reading CATHERINE. Catherine represented the next generation of conversational systems. It incorporated: larger knowledge bases (access to more information enabled richer answers); improved dialogue management (better tracking of conversation context and flow); more natural conversations (responses became more coherent and human-like). Example conversation: User: What can you tell me about the moon? Catherine: The moon is Earth's natural satellite. It influences tides and has been explored by many space missions. User: Who was the first person to walk on the moon? Catherine: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. User: Thank you! Catherine: You're welcome! Feel free to ask anything else. During this period AI researchers focused on: Knowledge Representation (structuring and organizing information so computers could use it); Expert Systems (building systems that captured human expert knowledge to solve complex problems); Natural Language Processing (enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language). Bottom: although not as widely recognized as ELIZA or PARRY, systems like Catherine demonstrated gradual improvements in conversational AI (a rising bar chart).

Infographic titled 5. 2000, EUGENE GOOSTMAN: A Milestone in Conversational AI. A cartoon of a boy with glasses captioned Eugene Goostman: the world's most famous chatbot designed as a 13-year-old boy. Eugene Goostman was designed as a 13-year-old Ukrainian boy. The young persona explained away grammatical mistakes and limited knowledge, making conversations seem more natural. In 2014, some reports claimed Eugene passed the Turing Test in a public competition, although this remains debated within the AI community. Example conversation: User: Where are you from? Eugene: I'm from Ukraine. I live in Odessa with my mom. And you? User: How old are you? Eugene: I'm 13 years old. Why do you think I'm so old? User: What do you like to do? Eugene: I like cats, playing football and programming. What about you? User: Do you have many friends? Eugene: Some. Not many. I'm a little shy in real life. Three points: by pretending to be a 13-year-old boy, Eugene's limitations seemed believable; people overlooked grammatical errors and knowledge gaps because of the persona; this raised important questions about what it really means for a machine to "think". Contribution: advanced conversational realism (Eugene showed that a well-designed persona, context-management, and clever responses can create engaging and human-like conversations); highlighted the strengths and limitations of the Turing Test (Eugene's case emphasized that passing the Turing Test does not necessarily mean true understanding or intelligence).

Infographic titled 6. 2011, CLEVERBOT: A Shift Toward Learning Chatbots, with the word Cleverbot and a smiling cartoon robot. Unlike earlier rule-based chatbots, Cleverbot learned from millions of previous conversations. Instead of relying only on predefined rules, it generated responses by comparing new inputs with its conversation database. This allowed Cleverbot to produce more human-like and varied conversations. Example conversation: User: Hello! Cleverbot: Hi there! How are you today? User: What do you think about AI? Cleverbot: AI is interesting. Do you think robots will take over the world? User: Maybe someday! Cleverbot: Someday is a long time. I just want to help people. User: What is the meaning of life? Cleverbot: That's a big question. Maybe it's to be happy and learn. Note: Cleverbot does not "understand" like humans; it predicts the most likely response based on patterns from past conversations. Contribution: learning from user interactions (Cleverbot improved by analyzing millions of real conversations from users worldwide); dynamic responses (it didn't follow fixed rules; it generated responses dynamically based on similar past conversations); large conversational memory (its massive database allowed for diverse topics, humor, opinions, questions, and more). Bottom line: this represented a shift from rule-based AI toward data-driven AI, paving the way for modern conversational AI systems.

slides.visual_text: Infographic titled 1990s: AI Rebounds with Real Applications. A photo of a man at a chessboard holding his head in his hands, labelled GARRY KASPAROV, facing a black machine labelled IBM Deep Blue, with two small flags and a chess clock on the table. Caption: 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeats world chess champion Garry Kasparov. A historic milestone that demonstrated the power of AI in complex strategic reasoning. Key developments in the 1990s: Natural Language Processing (NLP) makes progress: computers became better at understanding, interpreting, and generating human language. Speech Recognition makes progress: systems improved in recognizing spoken words, enabling hands-free interaction and voice-based services. Impact of the 1990s: the 1990s marked the resurgence of AI with practical applications and measurable results. It laid the foundation for AI to move from labs to real-world solutions.

Infographic titled 2000s: Machine Learning Matures. A picture of a laptop showing a glowing brain, with three floating panels: SVM (a scatter plot split by a dashed line), Decision Tree (a branching tree), and Ensemble Methods (several trees feeding into Voting / Averaging, then Prediction). Key developments in the 2000s (the same three points appear in two boxes): Advanced algorithms go mainstream: Support Vector Machines, decision trees, and ensemble methods become popular; these advanced algorithms improved predictions and performed well across many real-world tasks. 2006, Geoffrey Hinton coins "deep learning": this term highlighted the power (potential) of multi-layer neural networks to learn complex representations. Massive data and compute boost model accuracy: the growth of the internet and powerful hardware enabled training larger models on bigger datasets, delivering breakthrough performance. Impact of the 2000s: the 2000s transformed AI research into practical, scalable solutions. It set the stage for the deep learning revolution of the next decade.

Infographic titled 2010s: Deep Learning Revolution. Left, a vertical timeline. 2012, AlexNet wins ImageNet using CNNs: a convolutional neural network (CNN) called AlexNet dramatically outperformed previous methods, marking the start of the deep learning boom (a screen of dog photos labelled ALEXNET). 2014, GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks) introduced: GANs enabled machines to generate highly realistic data, opening new possibilities in image generation, creativity, and simulation (a loop diagram of a Generator and a Discriminator). 2016, AlphaGo defeats Go champion: deep reinforcement learning combined with tree search allowed AlphaGo to beat the world champion, a major milestone in AI (a Go board with an AlphaGo screen). Rise of voice assistants, facial recognition, and language models: AI technologies became part of everyday life through smart assistants, advanced vision systems, and powerful language models (icons of a smart speaker, a face scan and a chat bubble). Right, key developments and trends in the 2010s: Deep Learning Goes Mainstream (more layers, more data, and powerful GPUs made deep learning the dominant approach in AI); Big Data and Compute Power (explosion of data, cloud computing, and GPUs enabled training of large and complex models); AI on Mobile Devices (powerful models were optimized to run on phones, bringing AI to billions of users worldwide; a phone asking How can I help you?); Computer Vision Breakthroughs (huge advances in image classification, object detection, and facial recognition across industries; a street with people in detection boxes); Language Models Evolve (from RNNs to Transformers, models became better at understanding and generating language). Impact of the 2010s: deep learning became the engine of modern AI, achieving human-level performance in many tasks and transforming industries, products, and daily life.

slides.title: Turing Test & Logic Theorist: The Beginning of AI
slides.text:
Turing Test & Logic Theorist: The Beginning of AI
1. Turing Test (1950)
Proposed by: Alan Turing in his landmark paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”.
Purpose: To determine whether a machine can "think" or exhibit human-like intelligence.
How it works: A human judge converses with both a machine and another human via text. If the judge cannot reliably tell which is the machine, it is said to pass the test.
Significance:
Introduced the idea of machine intelligence.
Set the foundation for human-AI interaction studies.
Remains a philosophical and technical benchmark in AI ethics and design.

slides.title: 2. Logic Theorist (1956)
slides.text:
2. Logic Theorist (1956)
Developed by: Allen Newell & Herbert A. Simon at RAND Corporation.
What it did:
Proved 38 mathematical theorems from Principia Mathematica.
Was able to find more elegant proofs than humans for some theorems.
Significance:
Considered the first AI program.
Demonstrated that machines can perform symbolic reasoning.
Presented at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project—the official birth of AI as a field.

slides.title: Why These Matter
slides.text:
Why These Matter
Together, the Turing Test defined what it means for a machine to be intelligent, while the Logic Theorist proved it was possible. They kicked off the 70+ year journey that brought us from symbolic logic to today's generative AI.

slides.title: 3.AI Winters – Why progress stalled
slides.text:
3.AI Winters – Why progress stalled
The term "AI Winter" refers to periods when enthusiasm, funding, and progress in AI drastically declined—usually because of unmet expectations. There were two major AI Winters, and here’s a breakdown of why progress stalled:

bullets.text: The term "AI Winter" refers to periods when enthusiasm, funding, and progress in AI drastically declined—usually because of unmet expectations. There were two major AI Winters, and here’s a breakdown of why progress stalled:

slides.title: 1st AI Winter (Mid-1970s to Mid-1980s)
slides.text:
1st AI Winter (Mid-1970s to Mid-1980s)
Why It Happened:
Overpromising, underdelivering: Early AI systems (especially rule-based programs) failed to solve real-world problems.
Hardware limitations: Existing compute power was insufficient for complex tasks.
Brittle expert systems: Couldn't adapt or scale beyond narrow use-cases.
Government pullback: DARPA and UK’s Lighthill Report (1973) criticized AI’s limited results and halted major funding.
Impact:
AI research labs shut down.
Funding dropped dramatically.
AI lost credibility in both academia and industry.

slides.title: 2nd AI Winter (Late 1980s to Early 1990s)
slides.text:
2nd AI Winter (Late 1980s to Early 1990s)
Why It Happened:
Commercial expert systems failed: Businesses invested heavily, but maintenance costs soared, and performance lagged.
Market saturation: Too many companies entered the AI race without delivering real value.
AI became a ‘buzzword’: Hype exceeded actual capability, causing disillusionment.
Japan’s 5th Generation Project fell short of revolutionizing computing, damaging global AI momentum. Impact:
Venture capital disappeared.
Shift toward classical programming and simpler machine learning methods.
AI became absorbed into other domains like statistics, data mining, and robotics.

slides.title: What Changed After?
slides.text:
What Changed After?
Late 1990s–2000s: Rise of faster processors, larger datasets, and neural networks rebooted AI research.
2012+: Deep Learning breakthroughs (e.g., AlexNet) marked AI’s full comeback.

slides.title: The AI Comeback: Who Started It and How
slides.text:
The AI Comeback: Who Started It and How
1. Big Data – The Fuel
Key Enablers:
Google, Facebook, Amazon, Baidu, Microsoft
These tech giants began collecting massive user behavior, image, text, and speech data in the 2000s.
Notable Events & Figures:
Google’s Jeff Dean & Sanjay Ghemawat built the MapReduce and Google File System to process massive datasets.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) made storage and distributed computing affordable for startups and researchers. Impact:
Made it possible to train AI models on millions or billions of examples, enabling deep learning to generalize well.

slides.text:
The AI Comeback ……..Continue
2. GPUs – The Powerhouse
Key Innovators:
NVIDIA – particularly Ian Buck (developer of CUDA, 2006)
Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton – Used GPUs for deep learning in AlexNet (2012)
Game-Changer:
CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) let researchers write general- purpose programs on GPUs.
GPUs turned out to be 100x faster than CPUs for training deep neural networks.
Impact:
Training that used to take weeks with CPUs could now be done in days or hours.
Enabled rapid experimentation, breakthroughs in vision, NLP, and speech.

The AI Comeback ……..Continue
3. Deep Learning – The Brain Key Figures:
Geoffrey Hinton (University of Toronto) – Father of Deep Learning
Yann LeCun (Facebook AI) – Creator of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
Yoshua Bengio (Montreal) – Advanced sequence models and optimization Known as the “Godfathers of Deep Learning”, these three won the Turing Award in 2018 for their contributions.
Breakthrough Moment:
AlexNet (2012) – Won the ImageNet competition with 85% accuracy, 10% better than anyone before.
Used deep CNNs + ReLU activation + dropout + two GPUs.
Impact:
Sparked massive interest in neural networks.
Led to explosion of AI startups, AI labs (Google Brain, DeepMind, OpenAI), and real- world products.

slides.title: Key Highlights
slides.text:
Key Highlights
Markets are skyrocketing, with total AI market exceeding $279 b in 2024, and DL alone poised for $1+ trillion by 2034 (
Usage shifted from academic/government labs to industrial applications, then to widespread commercial use—culminating in consumer-grade tools and enterprise-level deployments.
Availability evolved from exclusive mainframes and specialized hardware to accessible cloud services (AWS, Azure, etc.) and later to freely available APIs and consumer software.
Compute & data advanced from basic mainframes to powerful GPU clusters; today’s architectures, like transformers, demand immense computational resources from hyperscalers .

slides.title: The AI Comeback
slides.text: The AI Comeback
slides.visual_text: A picture titled The AI Comeback: Big Data + GPUs + Deep Learning, a timeline running from 2000 to 2012 with three dots. Big Data: Google, Facebook, Amazon generate massive amounts of user data (cartoon faces labelled Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat). GPUs: in 2006, NVIDIA launches CUDA for general-purpose GPU computing (a cartoon face labelled Ian Buck). Deep Learning: in 2012, AlexNet achieves breakthrough results in image classification (cartoon faces labelled Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio).

slides.text:
Conclusion:
AI didn’t come back by accident. It
returned because of:
• Massive data availability (thanks to
the web)
• Affordable compute power (via GPUs)
• Powerful algorithms (deep neural
networks)
• This AI Renaissance, launched around
2012, laid the foundation for GPT,
DALL·E, AlphaFold, ChatGPT, and
many more.
